title: Netflix's Ted Sarandos Sits Down with Indian Writers as Streaming Giant Deepens India Bet
excerpt: The co-CEO's evening with screenwriters in Mumbai follows the launch of Netflix's NextGen India Writers' Program and a $2 billion content investment commitment.
body:
• Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos met with a group of Indian screenwriters in Mumbai to discuss the future of storytelling on the platform.
  • The meeting followed the launch of the NextGen India Writers' Program, which brings Netflix's global talent development initiative to India for the first time.
  • Netflix has committed over $2 billion to Indian content and logged more than 3 billion viewing hours from India, according to figures shared at the WAVES summit earlier this year.
  • Monika Shergill, Vice President of Content for Netflix India, joined Sarandos at the gathering.

Ted Sarandos spent an evening in Mumbai this week doing something Netflix's co-CEO rarely does in public: listening. The executive sat down with a group of Indian screenwriters for what the company described as an open conversation about the craft of storytelling, creative opportunities, and the future of Indian entertainment on the platform.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=-fpeWiq2GS0

Joined by Monika Shergill, Netflix India's Vice President of Content, Sarandos engaged writers in a discussion that the company framed as part of its broader effort to build creative partnerships by investing in writers and their ideas, rather than simply acquiring finished projects.

The NextGen India Writers' Program

The gathering comes on the heels of Netflix's launch of its NextGen India Writers' Program, which brings the company's global talent development initiative to India for the first time. The program is designed to identify and nurture emerging Indian writing talent, providing access to Netflix's development resources and creative infrastructure.

While Netflix has not disclosed the specific structure of the Indian program, its global NextGen initiative typically offers selected writers mentorship, development support, and a pathway to producing content for the platform. The India launch signals a shift from Netflix's earlier approach in the market, which relied heavily on established production houses and proven showrunners.

"Every great story begins with a unique creative voice."

— Netflix, describing its approach to the Indian writers' gathering

A $2 Billion Bet on India

Netflix's courtship of Indian writers comes against the backdrop of significant financial commitment to the market. At the WAVES global summit earlier this year, the company said it had invested more than $2 billion in Indian content and that India had generated over 3 billion viewing hours on the platform.

The company also launched Eyeline Studios in Hyderabad, a production facility designed to support Indian content creation at scale. These moves position Netflix to compete more aggressively with local streaming rivals, including Disney+ Hotstar, Amazon Prime Video, and Jio Cinema, in a market where the battle for subscribers increasingly hinges on the quality and volume of original Indian-language programming.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Netflix's deepening investment in Indian storytelling has practical implications. Indian-language content on the platform is available globally, and diaspora viewership represents a meaningful share of the audience for Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and Malayalam programming outside India.

The push to develop new writers — rather than relying solely on established names — could diversify the kinds of stories that reach international audiences. If the NextGen program produces writers who reflect a broader range of Indian experiences, including those of the diaspora itself, the content pipeline could shift in ways that resonate with audiences who have long felt underrepresented in both Indian and Western entertainment.

Sarandos's Mumbai visit, while largely symbolic, reinforces a message Netflix has been sending with increasing clarity: the company believes India is one of its most important growth markets, and it intends to compete for the country's best creative talent — starting with the people who write the stories.
